intro: Good writing is rewritten writing. In this lesson you edit like a professional: from the big picture down to the last comma, cutting words that add nothing and keeping spelling, terms, numbers and dates consistent. You also follow a house style guide and learn to give feedback that really helps a colleague, instead of just saying 'bagus kok'.
teachingNotes: Chain recap in one line each, don't re-teach: c1-professional-writing (cut filler: in order to → to, due to the fact that → because, make a decision regarding → decide on; active when the actor matters; one idea per sentence) and c2-complex-sentences (parallel lists, readable noun phrases, one meaning per sentence). At C2 there is no new grammar: this lesson is about the editor's process and habits. Explain terms the first time in plain Indonesian: edit (menyunting), proofread (pemeriksaan akhir untuk salah ketik), style guide / house style (gaya selingkung: aturan tulis yang dipilih sebuah kantor, penerbit atau jurnal), style sheet (daftar keputusan gaya untuk satu dokumen), redundancy (kata yang mengulang arti), feedback (masukan). Be honest: many choices (British or American spelling, the serial comma, Title Case or sentence case, the number rule) are not right or wrong in themselves; the error is mixing them in one document or ignoring the guide you were given. Test only clear cases: a rule stated in the prompt, a clearly redundant word, a clearly inconsistent term.

Objective concise-consistent. Levels of editing, big to small (names vary a little between publishers; the order doesn't): structural edit (purpose, missing parts, order of sections and paragraphs), line edit (each sentence: clarity, concision, tone, flow), copy-edit (correctness and consistency against a style guide: grammar, spelling, terms, numbers, dates, punctuation), proofread (last check of the final version: typos, missing words, page numbers, headings, links). Fix the big things first; edit your own text in separate passes and take a break before proofreading. Concision beyond C1: redundancy (return back → return, the end result / the final outcome → the result / the outcome, each and every → each or every, past history → history, merge together → merge, revert back → revert), empty openers (I would like to inform you that …, It is important to note that …, There are many people who … → Many people …), weak verb + noun (make an announcement → announce, carry out an investigation into → investigate, give an explanation of → explain). The node's common error: 'In order to be able to make a decision regarding the budget, we need more data' → 'To decide on the budget, we need more data.' Concise is not telegraphic or rude: keep please, thank you and full sentences; 'in order not to' is still useful. Consistency checklist: spelling variety (organise/organize, colour/color, centre/center, programme/program; British 'program' is only for computers), terminology (one term for one thing: customer, not client or user for the same people), tense (a report about the past stays in the past), person (we or the company), heading capitalisation (Title Case or sentence case), numbers (many style guides: one to nine in words, 10 and above in figures; figures for percentages, money and measurements; don't start a sentence with a figure; Chicago, for example, spells out numbers up to one hundred), dates (British 15 March 2026, American March 15, 2026; avoid 03/04/2026 internationally), the serial (Oxford) comma used or not used in every list, abbreviations defined at first use (micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs), then MSMEs).

Indonesian traps for concise-consistent: the school rule 'jangan mengulang kata yang sama' leads to elegant variation (pelanggan, konsumen, pembeli → customers, clients, users) that makes an English reader think of three groups; Indonesian pleonasm translated word for word (kembali lagi → return back; agar supaya → so that in order to); formal-letter openers (Dengan ini kami memberitahukan bahwa → We hereby inform you that → just say it); no tense marking, so tenses drift in long reports (Sales rose in March but fall in April); school books often teach British spelling while films and software default to American, so colour and color end up in the same report (check the spellchecker's language setting). Indonesian dates (15 Maret 2026) already follow the British order.

Objective style-guide. A style guide (gaya selingkung in Indonesian publishing) is the set of writing rules an organisation chooses so everything it publishes is consistent. Name well-known ones without quoting them: APA Style (psychology, education, social sciences, especially references), The Chicago Manual of Style (American book publishing, many humanities journals), the AP Stylebook (American news), the Guardian and Observer style guide and The Economist Style Guide (British journalism); Indonesian has EYD (formerly PUEBI). Guides differ (Chicago and APA use the serial comma; AP and the Guardian usually don't, except to avoid confusion), so the question is always: which guide does this document follow? Rules: the house style wins even over your own correct habit; read it before writing and keep it open while editing; check one rule at a time across the document (all dates, then all numbers); if the guide is silent, decide and record it in a style sheet. In practice items the rules are given in the prompt (a mini style guide); grade against those rules only. Indonesian habit: treating the house style as optional ('yang penting isinya'); some journals return a paper that ignores their format before anyone reads it.

Objective give-feedback. Useful feedback is specific (where and why: not just 'Good!' or 'Unclear'), prioritised (structure, missing information and the main argument first, sentences next, typos last: the levels of editing again; two or three key issues, not 40 comments) and kind and actionable (what to do next). Pattern: what works / what could be stronger / a suggestion. Phrase comments as questions or suggestions so the writer stays in charge: Could this paragraph come first? Consider cutting the first two sentences. Would a table make these figures easier to compare? What if you ended with the decision you need? Separate the person from the text: 'This sentence is hard to follow', not 'You're confusing'; I-statements help (I wasn't sure which project 'it' refers to). Indonesian habits, named kindly: very vague praise (bagus kok, sudah oke, mantap) that avoids sungkan but teaches nothing, and the red pen on everything (coret-coret semua, rewriting the text in your own style) that hides what matters. Questions work especially well with senior colleagues (Would it help to add the 2025 figures here?).

Limits and grading: no new grammar; any A0–C2 structure may appear. Don't teach typesetting, reference formats (how to write an APA citation) or proofreading symbols. In typed answers ignore capitals and punctuation, but where a rule about a date or a number is given, grade the format against that rule. For free rewrites and feedback comments, grade on meaning, concision, politeness and whether the comment says what to do, not on one wording; praise what works first, then suggest ONE more improvement. All people, organisations and figures are invented practice examples. Contexts: Bu Ani's NGO in Bandung (digital literacy workshops), Budi's reports for an e-commerce company in Surabaya, Rina's proposals, Pak Hasan and Dr. Wulan as senior colleagues. The lesson's own English uses British spelling.

keyPoints.title: Edit from big to small: concise and consistent
keyPoints.explanation: Edit in four levels, big to small: structural edit (order and missing parts), line edit (clear, concise sentences), copy-edit (correctness and consistency) and proofread (the last check for typos). Cut words that add nothing: redundancy (return back → return, the end result → the result), empty openers (I would like to inform you that …) and a weak verb + noun (carry out an investigation → investigate). Then make one choice and keep it everywhere: spelling variety, terms, tense, person, headings, numbers, dates, the serial comma and abbreviations.

examples.en: To decide on the budget, we need more data.
examples.id: Untuk memutuskan anggarannya, kita butuh data lebih banyak. (bukan In order to be able to make a decision regarding …)

examples.en: Please return the form by Friday.
examples.id: Mohon kembalikan formulirnya paling lambat Jumat. (bukan return back)

examples.en: Our customers in Medan rated the service highly, and most customers renewed.
examples.id: Pelanggan kami di Medan menilai layanannya tinggi, dan sebagian besar pelanggan memperpanjang. (satu istilah untuk satu hal)

id.title: Menyunting dari besar ke kecil: ringkas dan konsisten
id.explanation: Sunting dalam empat tingkat, dari besar ke kecil: structural edit (urutan dan bagian yang hilang), line edit (kalimat yang jelas dan ringkas), copy-edit (ketepatan dan konsistensi) dan proofread (pemeriksaan terakhir untuk salah ketik). Buang kata yang tidak menambah arti: redundansi (return back → return, the end result → the result), pembuka kosong (I would like to inform you that …) dan kata kerja lemah + kata benda (carry out an investigation → investigate). Lalu buat satu pilihan dan pakai di mana-mana: ejaan British atau Amerika, istilah, tense, sudut pandang (we/the company), judul bagian, angka, tanggal, serial comma dan singkatan.

keyPoints.title: Follow the house style guide
keyPoints.explanation: A style guide (house style) is the list of writing rules an organisation chooses: spelling, dates, numbers, commas, terms and headings. Well-known guides include APA, Chicago, AP, and the Guardian and Economist guides; many companies, journals and NGOs have their own. The house style wins, even when your own habit is also correct. Check one rule at a time across the document, and if the guide says nothing, decide and write it down in a style sheet.

examples.en: On 3 March 2026, four trainers ran workshops in Bandung, Garut and Bogor.
examples.id: Pada 3 Maret 2026, empat pelatih mengadakan lokakarya di Bandung, Garut dan Bogor. (tanggal British, four dalam kata, tanpa serial comma)

examples.en: The center offers courses in English, Mandarin, and Japanese.
examples.id: Pusat itu menawarkan kursus bahasa Inggris, Mandarin dan Jepang. (gaya Amerika: center, dengan serial comma)

id.title: Ikuti style guide (gaya selingkung)
id.explanation: Style guide (gaya selingkung) adalah daftar aturan menulis yang dipilih sebuah organisasi: ejaan, tanggal, angka, koma, istilah dan judul bagian. Yang terkenal antara lain APA, Chicago, AP, serta panduan The Guardian dan The Economist; banyak perusahaan, jurnal dan LSM punya aturan sendiri. Gaya selingkung yang menang, meskipun kebiasaanmu sendiri juga benar. Periksa satu aturan sekaligus di seluruh dokumen, dan kalau panduannya tidak mengatur sesuatu, putuskan lalu catat di style sheet (daftar keputusan gaya).

keyPoints.title: Feedback that helps the writer
keyPoints.explanation: Useful feedback is specific (where and why), prioritised (structure and missing information first, typos last) and kind and actionable (what to do next). A simple pattern: what works / what could be stronger / a suggestion. Write comments as questions or suggestions (Could this paragraph come first? Consider cutting …) and talk about the text, not the person (This sentence is hard to follow, not You're confusing). Avoid both vague praise (bagus kok) and the red pen on everything.

examples.en: The summary tells the director exactly what you need.
examples.id: Ringkasannya memberi tahu direktur persis apa yang kamu butuhkan. (yang sudah bagus, spesifik)
Bagaimana kalau paragraf ini ditaruh paling depan? (saran dalam bentuk pertanyaan)

examples.en: I wasn't sure which project 'it' refers to here.
examples.id: Saya kurang yakin 'it' di sini merujuk ke proyek yang mana. (tentang teksnya, bukan orangnya)

id.title: Feedback yang membantu penulis
id.explanation: Feedback yang berguna itu spesifik (di mana dan kenapa), berurutan prioritas (struktur dan informasi yang hilang dulu, salah ketik terakhir), serta sopan dan bisa ditindaklanjuti (apa yang harus dilakukan). Pola sederhana: yang sudah bagus / yang bisa lebih kuat / satu saran. Tulis komentar sebagai pertanyaan atau saran (Could this paragraph come first? Consider cutting …) dan bicarakan teksnya, bukan orangnya (This sentence is hard to follow, bukan You're confusing). Hindari pujian yang terlalu umum (bagus kok) maupun mencoret semuanya dengan tinta merah.

assessment.prompt:
Rina's report follows a style sheet that says: call the people who buy from us 'customers', every time. One word in this sentence breaks that rule. Write the word.
Our customers in Surabaya rated the app 4.5 out of 5, and most clients said that delivery was faster than last year.
acceptableAnswers: clients
client
assessment.rubric: Correct: clients (they are the same people as 'customers', so the style sheet's term must be used: most customers said …). 'client' = 100. 'customers' = 0 (that is the correct term). Any other word = 0.

assessment.prompt:
Make this sentence more concise: one word only repeats the meaning of the verb. Write the word to delete.
The two Bandung offices will merge together in January.
acceptableAnswers: together
the two bandung offices will merge in january
assessment.rubric: Correct: together (merge already means 'join together': The two Bandung offices will merge in January). The full sentence without 'together' = 100. 'two', 'will' or 'in January' = 0 (they carry meaning). Replacing merge with another verb but keeping 'together' (combine together) = 0.

assessment.prompt:
House style: write dates as day + month in words + year, with no comma and no 'st', 'nd', 'rd' or 'th' (example: 9 May 2026). Rewrite this date in the house style:
October 3rd, 2026

assessment.rubric: Correct: 3 October 2026 (capitals don't matter in grading). '03 October 2026' = 80 (right format, extra zero). '3rd October 2026' = 50 (right order, but the guide says no 'rd'). '3 Oct 2026' = 50 (month must be in full words). 'October 3, 2026', '3/10/2026' or '2026-10-03' = 0 (not the house format).

assessment.prompt:
House style: write numbers from one to nine in words and numbers from 10 upwards in figures. Rewrite the sentence in the house style:
Our team trained 8 teachers from 12 schools in Garut.
acceptableAnswers: our team trained eight teachers from 12 schools in garut
eight teachers from 12 schools
eight
assessment.rubric: Full: Our team trained eight teachers from 12 schools in Garut (8 → eight; 12 stays in figures). 'eight' alone = 100 (the only change needed). Writing 'twelve' as well = 40 (12 must stay in figures). Leaving both as figures = 0. 'eigth' = 70 (right rule, spelling slip).

assessment.prompt:
House style: British spelling. One word in this sentence uses American spelling. Write that word in British spelling.
The organisers will analyze the comments and send a summary to the centre next week.
acceptableAnswers: analyse
assessment.rubric: Correct: analyse (British -yse; American analyze). 'analyze' = 0 (unchanged). 'analise' = 30 (right idea, wrong spelling). Changing 'organisers' or 'centre' = 0 (they are already British).

assessment.rubric: Full: a question that starts with Could and keeps the action and the table: Could you put the budget table first? / Could the budget table come first? 'Could you change the table?' = 40 (polite, but no longer says what to do). A statement or an order (You must put …) = 0.

material.title: Four levels of editing: from big to small

blocks.text:
**Editing** (menyunting) is much more than finding typos. Professional editors work in **four levels**, from big to small:
- **1. Structural edit** (the big picture): Is the purpose clear? Is anything missing? Are the sections and paragraphs in the best order? *Put the recommendations first; the background is too long.*
- **2. Line edit** (sentence by sentence): Is every sentence clear, concise and in the right tone? *Cut 'It is important to note that'; split this 60-word sentence.*
- **3. Copy-edit** (correctness and consistency): grammar, spelling, terms, numbers, dates and punctuation, checked against a **style guide**. *'colour' on page 2 but 'color' on page 5: choose one.*
- **4. Proofread** (the final check, just before it goes out): typos, missing words, page numbers, headings, links. *'teh' → 'the'; the table on page 4 has no title.*
**Why the order matters:** there's no point polishing the commas in a paragraph that the structural edit will delete. Fix the big things first.
The names vary a little between publishers (some say *stylistic edit* for the line edit), but the big-to-small order is the same everywhere.
**On your own text:** do the levels in separate passes, and take a break before you proofread. After a night's sleep you see what you actually wrote, not what you meant to write.

id.text:
**Menyunting** (editing) jauh lebih dari sekadar mencari salah ketik. Editor profesional bekerja dalam **empat tingkat**, dari besar ke kecil:
- **1. Structural edit** (gambaran besar): Apakah tujuannya jelas? Ada yang hilang? Apakah urutan bagian dan paragrafnya sudah paling baik? *Taruh rekomendasinya di depan; latar belakangnya terlalu panjang.*
- **2. Line edit** (kalimat demi kalimat): Apakah setiap kalimat jelas, ringkas dan nadanya pas? *Buang 'It is important to note that'; pecah kalimat 60 kata ini.*
- **3. Copy-edit** (ketepatan dan konsistensi): tata bahasa, ejaan, istilah, angka, tanggal dan tanda baca, dicek dengan **style guide**. *Di halaman 2 'colour', di halaman 5 'color': pilih satu.*
- **4. Proofread** (pemeriksaan terakhir, tepat sebelum dikirim): salah ketik, kata yang hilang, nomor halaman, judul bagian, tautan. *'teh' → 'the'; tabel di halaman 4 belum punya judul.*
**Kenapa urutannya penting:** tidak ada gunanya merapikan koma di paragraf yang nanti dihapus saat structural edit. Perbaiki yang besar dulu.
Namanya sedikit berbeda antarpenerbit (ada yang menyebut line edit sebagai *stylistic edit*), tapi urutan dari besar ke kecil sama di mana-mana.
**Untuk tulisanmu sendiri:** kerjakan tiap tingkat dalam putaran terpisah, dan istirahatlah dulu sebelum proofread. Setelah tidur semalam, kamu melihat apa yang benar-benar kamu tulis, bukan apa yang ingin kamu tulis.

blocks.text: **Indonesian trap:** in many offices, *tolong dicek ya* means 'check the typos', so people start (and stop) at level 4. A report with perfect spelling can still have the wrong structure. When you ask for help, say which level you want: *Could you check the structure?* or *Could you just proofread it?*

id.text: **Jebakan bahasa Indonesia:** di banyak kantor, *tolong dicek ya* artinya 'cek salah ketik', jadi orang mulai (dan berhenti) di tingkat 4. Laporan dengan ejaan sempurna bisa saja strukturnya salah. Saat minta bantuan, sebutkan tingkat yang kamu mau: *Could you check the structure?* atau *Could you just proofread it?*

blocks.prompt: A colleague writes: 'On page 2 you wrote 15 March 2026, and on page 6 March 15, 2026. Our guide uses 15 March 2026.' Which level of editing is this?
blocks.explain: It's about **consistency** with the style guide (the date format), which is the copy-edit. A structural edit looks at the order and the missing parts; a line edit looks at how each sentence reads.

id.prompt: Seorang rekan menulis: 'On page 2 you wrote 15 March 2026, and on page 6 March 15, 2026. Our guide uses 15 March 2026.' Ini termasuk tingkat menyunting yang mana?
id.explain: Ini soal **konsistensi** dengan style guide (format tanggal), jadi termasuk copy-edit. Structural edit melihat urutan dan bagian yang hilang; line edit melihat bagaimana setiap kalimat terbaca.

id.title: Empat tingkat menyunting: dari besar ke kecil

material.title: Concise: cut words that add nothing

blocks.text:
**Quick recap (C1):** you already cut filler: *in order to* → *to*, *due to the fact that* → *because*, *make a decision regarding* → *decide on*. So *In order to be able to make a decision regarding the budget, we need more data* → *To decide on the budget, we need more data.*
At C2, an editor looks for three more kinds of extra words.
**1. Redundancy** (kata yang mengulang arti): the second word repeats the first.
- *return back* → **return** (return already means 'go or give back')
- *the end result*, *the final outcome* → **the result**, **the outcome**
- *each and every* → **each** or **every**
- *past history* → **history**; *revert back* → **revert**
**2. Empty openers:** the sentence starts long before the point.
- *I would like to inform you that the office is closed on Friday* → **The office is closed on Friday.**
- *It is important to note that …* → delete it, or say why it matters.
- *There are many people who prefer …* → **Many people prefer …**
**3. A weak verb + a noun** that hides the real verb:
- *make an announcement* → **announce**; *carry out an investigation into* → **investigate**; *give an explanation of* → **explain**; *make a recommendation* → **recommend**
**Concise is not rude.** Keep *please*, *thank you* and full sentences: *Meeting → Thu* is shorter, but not better in an email to a client. And some 'extra' words do a job: *in order not to miss the deadline* reads more clearly than *not to miss the deadline*. Cut a word only if the meaning and the tone stay the same.

id.text:
**Ulasan singkat (C1):** kamu sudah membuang kata pengisi (filler): *in order to* → *to*, *due to the fact that* → *because*, *make a decision regarding* → *decide on*. Jadi *In order to be able to make a decision regarding the budget, we need more data* → *To decide on the budget, we need more data.*
Di C2, editor mencari tiga jenis kata berlebih lagi.
**1. Redundansi** (kata yang mengulang arti): kata kedua mengulang kata pertama.
- *return back* → **return** (return sudah berarti 'kembali' atau 'mengembalikan')
- *the end result*, *the final outcome* → **the result**, **the outcome**
- *each and every* → **each** atau **every**
- *past history* → **history**; *revert back* → **revert**
**2. Pembuka kosong:** kalimatnya mulai jauh sebelum intinya.
- *I would like to inform you that the office is closed on Friday* → **The office is closed on Friday.**
- *It is important to note that …* → hapus, atau jelaskan kenapa penting.
- *There are many people who prefer …* → **Many people prefer …**
**3. Kata kerja lemah + kata benda** yang menyembunyikan kata kerja aslinya:
- *make an announcement* → **announce**; *carry out an investigation into* → **investigate**; *give an explanation of* → **explain**; *make a recommendation* → **recommend**
**Ringkas bukan berarti kasar.** Tetap pakai *please*, *thank you* dan kalimat lengkap: *Meeting → Thu* memang lebih pendek, tapi tidak lebih baik dalam email ke klien. Dan ada kata 'tambahan' yang punya tugas: *in order not to miss the deadline* lebih jelas daripada *not to miss the deadline*. Buang kata hanya kalau arti dan nadanya tetap sama.

blocks.text: **Indonesian trap: doubled words.** Indonesian has its own pairs that do one job: *kembali lagi*, *agar supaya*, *demi untuk*. Translated word for word, they become English redundancy: *return back*, *so that in order to* ✗ (→ *so that* or *to*). Formal letters add another: *Dengan ini kami memberitahukan bahwa …* → *We hereby inform you that …*: in a modern email, just say the news.

id.text: **Jebakan bahasa Indonesia: kata ganda.** Bahasa Indonesia punya pasangan kata yang melakukan satu tugas: *kembali lagi*, *agar supaya*, *demi untuk*. Kalau diterjemahkan kata per kata, jadinya redundansi dalam bahasa Inggris: *return back*, *so that in order to* ✗ (→ *so that* atau *to*). Surat resmi menambah satu lagi: *Dengan ini kami memberitahukan bahwa …* → *We hereby inform you that …*: dalam email modern, langsung saja sampaikan beritanya.

blocks.prompt: Which is the best edit of: 'We would like to inform all customers that on the day of Sunday the app will be unavailable.'
options: The app will be unavailable on Sunday.
We would like to inform customers that on Sunday the app will be unavailable.
blocks.explain: The first keeps the full meaning in a polite, complete sentence and cuts the empty opener and *the day of*. The second still has the opener; the third is so short that it sounds rude and unclear in a message to customers.

id.prompt: Mana suntingan terbaik untuk: 'We would like to inform all customers that on the day of Sunday the app will be unavailable.'

material.title: Consistency: one choice, all the way through

blocks.text:
A reader notices when a text changes its mind. If page 2 says *customers* and page 5 says *clients*, they wonder: are these different people? **Consistency** means: make a choice, then keep it everywhere. Check these:
- **Spelling variety:** British (*organise, colour, centre, programme*) or American (*organize, color, center, program*) all the way through. (In British English, *program* is only for computers.) Spellcheckers are often set to US English by default: check the language setting.
- **Terminology** (istilah): one name for one thing. If the people who buy from you are *customers*, don't switch to *clients* or *users*.
- **Tense:** a report about last year stays in the past (*Sales rose …, complaints fell …*). Don't drift into the present halfway through a paragraph.
- **Person:** *we* or *the company* (or *PT Maju*): choose one voice for the document.
- **Headings:** **Title Case** (*Annual Sales Report*: main words start with a capital) or **sentence case** (*Annual sales report*: only the first word and names). Both are fine; mixing them isn't.
- **Numbers:** many style guides write **one to nine in words** and **10 and above in figures** (*three branches, 12 staff*), but use figures for percentages, money and measurements (*5%, Rp5 million, 3 km*). Others differ: Chicago, for example, spells out numbers up to one hundred. Don't start a sentence with a figure: *Twelve staff …*, not *12 staff …*
- **Dates:** British **15 March 2026** or American **March 15, 2026**. Avoid *03/04/2026* in international documents: British readers see 3 April, American readers see March 4.
- **The serial (Oxford) comma:** the comma before *and* at the end of a list: *Jakarta, Bandung, and Surabaya* (with) or *Jakarta, Bandung and Surabaya* (without). Use it or don't, but the same way in every list.
- **Abbreviations:** write the full form the first time with the short form in brackets, then use the short form: *micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs)* … later just *MSMEs*.
None of these choices is 'the correct one'. The mistake is mixing them.

id.text:
Pembaca sadar kalau sebuah teks 'berubah pikiran'. Kalau halaman 2 menulis *customers* dan halaman 5 *clients*, mereka bertanya-tanya: apakah ini orang yang berbeda? **Konsistensi** artinya: buat satu pilihan, lalu pakai di mana-mana. Periksa hal-hal ini:
- **Ragam ejaan:** British (*organise, colour, centre, programme*) atau Amerika (*organize, color, center, program*) dari awal sampai akhir. (Dalam British English, *program* hanya untuk program komputer.) Pemeriksa ejaan sering otomatis disetel ke English (US): cek pengaturan bahasanya.
- **Istilah** (terminology): satu nama untuk satu hal. Kalau orang yang membeli darimu disebut *customers*, jangan berganti ke *clients* atau *users*.
- **Tense:** laporan tentang tahun lalu tetap memakai bentuk lampau (*Sales rose …, complaints fell …*). Jangan bergeser ke bentuk sekarang di tengah paragraf.
- **Sudut pandang:** *we* atau *the company* (atau *PT Maju*): pilih satu suara untuk seluruh dokumen.
- **Judul bagian:** **Title Case** (*Annual Sales Report*: kata-kata utama diawali huruf kapital) atau **sentence case** (*Annual sales report*: hanya kata pertama dan nama). Keduanya boleh; mencampurnya yang tidak boleh.
- **Angka:** banyak style guide menulis **one sampai nine dengan kata** dan **10 ke atas dengan angka** (*three branches, 12 staff*), tapi memakai angka untuk persen, uang dan ukuran (*5%, Rp5 million, 3 km*). Ada juga yang berbeda: Chicago, misalnya, menulis angka sampai one hundred dengan kata. Jangan membuka kalimat dengan angka: *Twelve staff …*, bukan *12 staff …*
- **Tanggal:** British **15 March 2026** atau Amerika **March 15, 2026**. Hindari *03/04/2026* dalam dokumen internasional: pembaca British membacanya 3 April, pembaca Amerika 4 Maret.
- **Serial (Oxford) comma:** koma sebelum *and* di akhir daftar: *Jakarta, Bandung, and Surabaya* (dengan) atau *Jakarta, Bandung and Surabaya* (tanpa). Boleh dipakai atau tidak, asal sama di setiap daftar.
- **Singkatan:** tulis bentuk lengkapnya pertama kali dengan singkatan dalam kurung, lalu pakai singkatannya: *micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs)* … berikutnya cukup *MSMEs*.
Tidak ada satu pilihan yang 'paling benar'. Kesalahannya adalah mencampur.

blocks.text: **Indonesian trap: 'jangan mengulang kata yang sama'.** At school you probably learnt to vary your words so a text doesn't sound boring: *pelanggan*, then *konsumen*, then *pembeli*. In English reports, contracts and instructions, that variety confuses: the reader thinks *customers*, *clients* and *users* are three different groups. Keep one term for one thing (in stories and essays, variety is fine). Two more: Indonesian has no tense marking, so tenses drift in long reports (*Sales rose in March, but in April they fall* ✗): check every verb in a paragraph about the past. And school books often teach British spelling while films and software use American, so *colour* and *color* end up in the same report. Good news: Indonesian dates (*15 Maret 2026*) already follow the British order.

id.text: **Jebakan bahasa Indonesia: 'jangan mengulang kata yang sama'.** Di sekolah kamu mungkin belajar mengganti-ganti kata supaya teks tidak membosankan: *pelanggan*, lalu *konsumen*, lalu *pembeli*. Dalam laporan, kontrak dan petunjuk berbahasa Inggris, variasi itu membingungkan: pembaca mengira *customers*, *clients* dan *users* adalah tiga kelompok berbeda. Pakai satu istilah untuk satu hal (dalam cerita dan esai, variasi boleh). Dua lagi: bahasa Indonesia tidak menandai tense, jadi tense sering bergeser dalam laporan panjang (*Sales rose in March, but in April they fall* ✗): periksa setiap kata kerja dalam paragraf tentang masa lalu. Dan buku sekolah sering mengajarkan ejaan British, sementara film dan perangkat lunak memakai ejaan Amerika, sehingga *colour* dan *color* muncul di laporan yang sama. Kabar baiknya: tanggal Indonesia (*15 Maret 2026*) sudah mengikuti urutan British.

blocks.prompt: Which sentence from a report about 2025 is consistent?
options: In 2025 the clinic treated 4,000 patients and opens a second branch.
In 2025 the clinic treated 4,000 patients and opened a second branch.
blocks.explain: Both actions happened in 2025, so both verbs are past: *treated … opened*. The first drifts into the present (*opens*) halfway through.

id.prompt: Kalimat mana dari laporan tentang tahun 2025 yang konsisten?
id.explain: Kedua tindakan terjadi pada 2025, jadi kedua kata kerjanya lampau: *treated … opened*. Kalimat pertama bergeser ke bentuk sekarang (*opens*) di tengah jalan.

id.title: Konsistensi: satu pilihan, dari awal sampai akhir

blocks.text:
A **style guide** (in Indonesian publishing: **gaya selingkung**) is a list of writing rules that an organisation chooses so that everything it publishes looks and sounds the same. It answers the questions of the last section once, for everybody: British or American? Which date format? Serial comma or not? Which word for our customers?
**Some well-known style guides:**
- **APA Style** (American Psychological Association): psychology, education and the social sciences, especially for references.
- **The Chicago Manual of Style:** American book publishing and many humanities journals.
- **The AP Stylebook:** American news agencies and newspapers.
- **The Guardian and Observer style guide** and **The Economist Style Guide:** British journalism.
Universities, journals, ministries, NGOs and companies often have a short **house style** of their own, sometimes just one page. (Indonesian has its own rules too: EYD, earlier called PUEBI.) The guides don't all agree: Chicago and APA use the serial comma, while AP and the Guardian usually leave it out. So always ask: **which guide does this document follow?**
**How to follow one:**
- **The house style wins**, even when your own habit is also correct. If the guide says *organize* and you learnt *organise*, write *organize*.
- Read it **before** you write, keep it open while you edit, and check **one rule at a time** across the whole document: all the dates, then all the numbers.
- If the guide says nothing about something, decide, write your decision down in a **style sheet** (daftar keputusan gaya untuk satu dokumen) and keep to it.
**Before and after.** Bu Ani's NGO guide says: British spelling; dates like 15 March 2026; one to nine in words; no serial comma; call the people on the course *participants*.
- Before: *On March 3, 2026, 4 trainers organized workshops in Bandung, Garut, and Bogor for 120 trainees.*
- After: *On 3 March 2026, four trainers organised workshops in Bandung, Garut and Bogor for 120 participants.*
Five changes: the date, the number, the spelling, the serial comma and the term.

id.text:
**Style guide** (dalam dunia penerbitan Indonesia: **gaya selingkung**) adalah daftar aturan menulis yang dipilih sebuah organisasi supaya semua yang diterbitkannya terlihat dan terdengar seragam. Panduan ini menjawab pertanyaan-pertanyaan di bagian sebelumnya sekali saja, untuk semua orang: British atau Amerika? Format tanggal yang mana? Pakai serial comma atau tidak? Kata apa untuk pelanggan kita?
**Beberapa style guide yang terkenal:**
- **APA Style** (American Psychological Association): psikologi, pendidikan dan ilmu sosial, terutama untuk daftar pustaka.
- **The Chicago Manual of Style:** penerbitan buku di Amerika dan banyak jurnal humaniora.
- **The AP Stylebook:** kantor berita dan surat kabar Amerika.
- **The Guardian and Observer style guide** dan **The Economist Style Guide:** jurnalisme Inggris.
Universitas, jurnal, kementerian, LSM dan perusahaan sering punya **gaya selingkung** sendiri yang pendek, kadang hanya satu halaman. (Bahasa Indonesia juga punya aturannya: EYD, dulu disebut PUEBI.) Panduan-panduan ini tidak selalu sepakat: Chicago dan APA memakai serial comma, sedangkan AP dan The Guardian biasanya tidak. Jadi selalu tanyakan: **dokumen ini mengikuti panduan yang mana?**
**Cara mengikutinya:**
- **Gaya selingkung yang menang**, meskipun kebiasaanmu sendiri juga benar. Kalau panduannya bilang *organize* dan kamu terbiasa *organise*, tulis *organize*.
- Baca **sebelum** menulis, biarkan terbuka saat menyunting, dan periksa **satu aturan sekaligus** di seluruh dokumen: semua tanggal dulu, lalu semua angka.
- Kalau panduannya tidak mengatur sesuatu, putuskan, catat keputusanmu di **style sheet** (daftar keputusan gaya untuk satu dokumen), lalu patuhi.
**Sebelum dan sesudah.** Panduan LSM Bu Ani: ejaan British; tanggal seperti 15 March 2026; one sampai nine dengan kata; tanpa serial comma; orang yang ikut kursus disebut *participants*.
- Sebelum: *On March 3, 2026, 4 trainers organized workshops in Bandung, Garut, and Bogor for 120 trainees.*
- Sesudah: *On 3 March 2026, four trainers organised workshops in Bandung, Garut and Bogor for 120 participants.*
Lima perubahan: tanggal, angka, ejaan, serial comma dan istilah.

blocks.text: **Indonesian habit: 'yang penting isinya'.** It's tempting to treat the house style as optional decoration. To an editor or a journal, ignoring it looks careless, and some journals send a paper back before anyone reads it if it doesn't follow their format. Five minutes with the guide saves a whole round of corrections.

id.text: **Kebiasaan: 'yang penting isinya'.** Gampang menganggap gaya selingkung sebagai hiasan yang boleh diabaikan. Bagi editor atau jurnal, mengabaikannya terlihat ceroboh, dan ada jurnal yang mengembalikan naskah sebelum dibaca kalau formatnya tidak sesuai. Lima menit membaca panduan menghemat satu putaran revisi.

blocks.prompt: House style: American spelling, and use the serial comma. Which sentence follows it?
options: The center offers courses in English, Mandarin, and Japanese.
The centre offers courses in English, Mandarin and Japanese.
The center offers courses in English, Mandarin and Japanese.
blocks.explain: American spelling is *center*, and the serial comma is the comma before *and*: *Mandarin, and Japanese*. The second is British with no serial comma; the third has the right spelling but no serial comma.

id.prompt: Gaya selingkung: ejaan Amerika, dan pakai serial comma. Kalimat mana yang mengikutinya?
id.explain: Ejaan Amerika adalah *center*, dan serial comma adalah koma sebelum *and*: *Mandarin, and Japanese*. Pilihan kedua British tanpa serial comma; yang ketiga ejaannya benar tapi tanpa serial comma.

blocks.text:
When a colleague asks *Could you look at my draft?*, they want help to make it better. Useful **feedback** (masukan) is:
- **Specific:** say where and why. *Good!* or *Unclear* on its own doesn't help. → *The second paragraph works well because each sentence gives one figure.* / *I got lost in the third paragraph: I wasn't sure which project 'it' refers to.*
- **Prioritised:** big issues first (structure, missing information, the main argument), then sentences, and typos last: the levels of editing again. If the structure needs work, don't send 40 comma corrections; name the two or three issues that matter most.
- **Kind and actionable:** polite, and clear about what to do next. *This is weak* ✗ → *Adding last year's figure would show how big the rise is.*
**A simple pattern: what works / what could be stronger / a suggestion.**
- *What works:* The summary tells the director exactly what you need.
- *What could be stronger:* The budget section doesn't show a total.
- *A suggestion:* Could you add a total row at the bottom of the table?
**Phrase comments as questions or suggestions**, so the writer stays in charge of their own text: *Could this paragraph come first?* · *Consider cutting the first two sentences: the point starts in the third.* · *Would a table make these figures easier to compare?* · *What if you ended with the decision you need?*
**Talk about the text, not the person:** *This sentence is hard to follow* ✓, not *You're confusing* ✗. Sentences with *I* help: *I wasn't sure …*, *As a reader, I expected …*

id.text:
Saat rekan bertanya *Could you look at my draft?*, mereka ingin dibantu supaya tulisannya lebih baik. **Feedback** (masukan) yang berguna itu:
- **Spesifik:** sebutkan di mana dan kenapa. *Good!* atau *Unclear* saja tidak membantu. → *The second paragraph works well because each sentence gives one figure.* / *I got lost in the third paragraph: I wasn't sure which project 'it' refers to.*
- **Berurutan prioritas:** masalah besar dulu (struktur, informasi yang hilang, argumen utama), lalu kalimat, dan salah ketik terakhir: lagi-lagi tingkat menyunting. Kalau strukturnya perlu diperbaiki, jangan kirim 40 koreksi koma; sebutkan dua atau tiga masalah yang paling penting.
- **Sopan dan bisa ditindaklanjuti:** santun, dan jelas apa yang harus dilakukan berikutnya. *This is weak* ✗ → *Adding last year's figure would show how big the rise is.*
**Pola sederhana: yang sudah bagus / yang bisa lebih kuat / satu saran.**
- *What works:* The summary tells the director exactly what you need.
- *What could be stronger:* The budget section doesn't show a total.
- *A suggestion:* Could you add a total row at the bottom of the table?
**Tulis komentar sebagai pertanyaan atau saran**, supaya penulis tetap memegang kendali atas teksnya: *Could this paragraph come first?* · *Consider cutting the first two sentences: the point starts in the third.* · *Would a table make these figures easier to compare?* · *What if you ended with the decision you need?*
**Bicarakan teksnya, bukan orangnya:** *This sentence is hard to follow* ✓, bukan *You're confusing* ✗. Kalimat dengan *I* membantu: *I wasn't sure …*, *As a reader, I expected …*

blocks.text: **Two Indonesian habits.** 1) **Vague praise:** *bagus kok*, *sudah oke*, *mantap*. It's kind (and it avoids feeling *sungkan*), but the writer learns nothing and the problems stay. Name one thing that works, and why. 2) **The red pen on everything** (*coret-coret semua*), like a strict school teacher: every comma marked and the text rewritten in your own style. The writer can't see what matters and may feel attacked. Choose the two or three changes that make the biggest difference, and leave matters of taste alone. With a senior colleague, questions work especially well: *Would it help to add the 2025 figures here?*

id.text: **Dua kebiasaan orang Indonesia.** 1) **Pujian yang terlalu umum:** *bagus kok*, *sudah oke*, *mantap*. Niatnya baik (dan menghindari rasa *sungkan*), tapi penulis tidak belajar apa-apa dan masalahnya tetap ada. Sebutkan satu hal yang sudah bagus, dan kenapa. 2) **Tinta merah di mana-mana** (*coret-coret semua*), seperti guru yang galak: setiap koma ditandai dan teksnya ditulis ulang dengan gayamu sendiri. Penulis tidak bisa melihat mana yang penting dan bisa merasa diserang. Pilih dua atau tiga perubahan yang paling berpengaruh, dan biarkan hal yang soal selera saja. Dengan rekan yang lebih senior, pertanyaan sangat cocok: *Would it help to add the 2025 figures here?*

blocks.prompt: Which comment is about the text, not the person, and tells the writer what to do?
options: You always write sentences that are far too long.
This sentence has 58 words: could you split it after 'budget'?
blocks.explain: The second points to one sentence, says why (58 words) and suggests a clear action, as a question. The first is about the person (*You always …*); the third is too vague to act on.

id.prompt: Komentar mana yang membahas teksnya, bukan orangnya, dan memberi tahu penulis apa yang harus dilakukan?
id.explain: Pilihan kedua menunjuk satu kalimat, menyebut alasannya (58 kata) dan menyarankan tindakan yang jelas, dalam bentuk pertanyaan. Pilihan pertama membahas orangnya (*You always …*); yang ketiga terlalu umum untuk ditindaklanjuti.
